title: In the hand of God (Wisdom 3:1–9)
hookLine: the souls of the just are in the hand of God, read at many funerals

cards: "But the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them."
It's one of the readings a family may choose for a Catholic funeral, so if you've heard it, it may have been from a lectern, near a coffin, on a hard day. Some people hear it only there.
It comes from one of the seven books we met this week: the Book of Wisdom, a book that argues with people who think death ends everything.

teach.b: Wisdom speaks in the voice of a king who prayed for wisdom, the voice tradition gives to Solomon, though the book never names him.
It comes down to us in Greek, and some readers place its writer among the Greek-speaking Jews of Alexandria.

Chapter two lets the other side speak first, and they sound very modern. Life is short and then nothing. Let's enjoy ourselves, and if a just man makes us feel bad, let's crush him and see if his God saves him.
Chapter three answers. The souls of the just are in the hand of God.
And the Douay goes on: "In the sight of the unwise they seemed to die: and their departure was taken for misery: And their going away from us, for utter destruction: but they are in peace." Seemed.
From outside, it looks like the end. But they are in peace. Their hope, the writer says, is full of immortality.

teach.h: GOLD IN THE FURNACE, SPARKS IN THE REEDS.
teach.b: God tested them like gold in a furnace and received them like an offering, and at their visitation the just shall shine, and run to and fro like sparks among the reeds.
Here hope reaches past death in so many words, which is why the Church reaches for it at funerals and on the feasts of martyrs.
And the image is plain: a hand. Not a cloud, not a distant throne. A hand, the way you'd hold something small and precious so nothing can get at it.

how: Wisdom 3:1–9 is among the Old Testament readings a family may choose for a Catholic funeral, and it is also read on feasts of martyrs and on All Souls' Day.

games.q: you're the writer of Wisdom. you've just let the ungodly speak: life is short and then nothing. how do you answer them?
o: agree, and tell people to enjoy life while they can.
say the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and they are in peace.
say nothing; leave the argument there.
games.why: they seemed to die; their going was taken for destruction; but they are in peace. their hope is full of immortality.

practice: Let one person who has died come to mind, a grandparent, a friend, a child, someone whose funeral you remember or missed, and say their name quietly.

Picture their hands, then picture those hands held in a larger hand, safe, so nothing can touch them now. If you pray, you can pray for them; Catholics have an old prayer for this that begins eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord.
If you don't, just hold their name for a while.

wordCard.voice: Immortality. The hope Wisdom says is full and unshaken for the just who have died: they seemed to die, but they are in peace. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: in the hand of God, the words of Wisdom 3:1 in the Greek text.

carryVoice: Your line: they are in peace. Held in a hand, where nothing can get at them. See you tomorrow.
